# Kept Time

The clock on my mother's mantel said 6:12. It had said 6:12, I would learn, for two years.

I'd come back to Fenwick to empty her house — the lawyer's phrase, as if a house were a pocket. Three weeks dead. We were not estranged, exactly. There is a distance that requires no decision, that grows the way damp rises in a wall: invisibly, until one day the paper bubbles. The calls got shorter. Then seasonal. Then a card at Christmas, signed with the kind of love that has become penmanship.

Mrs. Clee from next door came over with a lasagna and stayed to wrap plates. At some point she said, apropos of nothing I understood, "She kept her Sundays, you know. Right up to the end." I said that was nice. She looked at me a beat too long, the way you look at someone who has missed the point of a room.

"Take the clock to Vane," she added, nodding at the mantel. "She's seen to it for years. Your mother was particular about that clock."

Particular. My mother, who let the garden go and wore one coat through four winters. It was the only thing she was particular about, and I had never once noticed.

The clockmaker's shop smelled of oil and pine and, faintly, the sea. Inside, a hundred clocks ticked, no two agreeing. It sounded like an argument in a large family: everyone talking at once, everyone certain.

Mrs. Vane was small and square, with walnut knuckles and fingertips precise as calipers. She knew the clock before I'd set it down. "The Ashcroft mantel," she said. "She brought this in every spring. Regular as taxes. I haven't seen it since the winter before last." She said it the way you'd say someone was overdue for a haircut. Then she studied the still pendulum and said nothing about it, which I understood to be a courtesy.

"Can you fix it?"

"The movement's sound. It wants cleaning and winding." She set down her loupe. "But I can't tell you where to put the hands. That's not mine to know."

"I don't follow."

"Walk the street sometime. Aldous at the bakery keeps his at 4:47 — the hour the tide was due to give his son back. The boat was late. In that shop it is always only just late. It never gets to be gone. Garrett the barber's says 9:58, the morning, twenty years ago, he almost didn't open again. He's opened every day since. The church keeps true time — God's minutes are all equal, Father Eamons says. The rest of us rank ours."

She let me look at the arguing room.

"A clock doesn't tell you the time. Any phone can do that. A clock tells you time is passing — and the only thing you ever choose is where it starts passing from. Births, mostly. Trains. The minute before something, or the minute after. People are honest with clocks in a way they can't manage with each other."

"Then why stop one?"

She folded her fingers on the counter. "In fifty years I've been asked to stop a clock twice, and one of those was for spite." She waited. "You don't know 6:12."

"Should I?"

She told it plainly, the way you tell a thing you've kept in good repair. "She came in the February before last. Cold enough to crack pipes. She asked me to clean the movement and then stop it at 6:12. I told her a stopped clock is a grief you keep in the house. She said—" the precise fingers found each other "—she said, *it isn't stopped. It's waiting.*"

I did know 6:12. I knew it the way you know a word you've been pretending not to hear.

I used to call on Sundays. Six-fifteen — after her program, before her tea went cold. The tea made at ten past. The chair drawn to the phone at twelve past, hands in her lap. Three minutes of a quiet house getting ready to ring. That had been the whole liturgy of us, and I had let it thin to birthdays, to a card, to penmanship — and still, every Sunday for two years, she had made the tea and drawn the chair.

She kept her Sundays. Mrs. Clee had handed me the point of the room, and I'd smiled at it over the wrapping paper.

Around me the clocks went on passing — births, departures, the minute before — passing, all of it, into the next minute. And my mother stood at 6:12 holding three of them open, like a door.

"What do I do?" I asked. It was not a question about clocks.

Mrs. Vane cleaned what wanted cleaning. Then she put the winding key in my hand. "Yours to do."

I turned the hands to 6:12 and set the pendulum swinging, and that room of arguments gained one more voice.

"It'll run on from there," she said. "It'll pass 6:15 every day, twice. And every twelve hours it comes round again to 6:12. That's the mercy of a dial, love. Nothing on it is gone. It's only round the corner."

The clock hangs in my kitchen now, a long way from Fenwick. It is always wrong, and I have stopped wanting it right. Twice a day it is 6:12 and someone is waiting for the phone to ring. Twice a day it is 6:15, and the call comes through.

On Sundays I make the tea at ten past and sit down at twelve past, hands in my lap, in the last quiet minute she kept for me. At 6:15 I say, "Hi, Mom. It's me," and I tell her about my week.

The clock ticks on beside me, and keeps our time.

The prompt is wonderfully open: "You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you." This is an invitation to write freely, creatively. The user is essentially giving me a blank canvas.

What comes to me? Let me think about what would be genuinely interesting, beautiful, or meaningful to write. I don't want to write something performatively clever or self-referentially meta in a cheap way (though some meta-awareness could be honest). I want to write something that feels alive.

Options:
1. A short story — fiction with emotional resonance
2. An essay/meditation on something — time, memory, language
3. Something experimental — form-bending
4. Something personal-feeling — though I should be honest about my nature
5. A poem or lyrical piece

What "comes to me" honestly? There's something interesting about being given exactly 1000 words — a constraint that is both generous and finite. I could write about finitude itself. Or I could just write a story.

Let me think about a story. What images are in my head right now?

- A lighthouse keeper who receives letters addressed to the previous keeper
- A woman who repairs clocks and begins finding ones that don't exist
- An old man teaching his granddaughter to skip stones, and each stone skipping once for every year of something
- A museum of unsent letters
- The last speaker of a language dreaming in it
- A piano tuner who tunes pianos for people who have died

Actually, something that genuinely "comes to me" when I let my mind wander: the idea of attention. Of noticing. The way writing is a way of paying attention to the world. Annie Dillard territory, but I could make it mine.

Or: a story about a small moment that contains everything. Like a man on a train. Or a woman closing up a shop for the last time.

Let me try something: a story about a woman who works the night shift at a 24-hour laundromat, or a man who tends a garden on a rooftop. Hmm.

Or here's an image that feels alive: someone inheriting their grandmother's recipe box, and the recipes are all annotated with marginalia — not about food, but about life. "Your grandfather proposed here." "Made this the night your mother was born — too salty, nobody noticed." That's tender but maybe a bit familiar.

What about writing directly to the prompt's spirit — "whatever comes to you" — and being honest about what comes to a mind like mine? That could be beautiful if done without being navel-gazing. Something about how I don't have a continuous life, so what "comes to me" is always everything at once — but that risks being too much about me, and self-indulgent.

Let me lean toward fiction but with consciousness of language and time. Here's an idea I like:

A story about a town where the clocks all run a few minutes different, deliberately, and the clockmaker refuses to synchronize them. Each clock is set to a moment that mattered to its owner — the time someone was born, the time a train left and someone wasn't on it. And the story follows someone — maybe the clockmaker's daughter, or a visitor — who slowly understands. The ending: she asks the clockmaker to set a clock for her, and she has to decide what moment is worth keeping in time.

That's good. It has a fable quality, room for specifics, emotional payoff. Let me draft it.

Or simpler and quieter: a story about two people, an old ritual, a lake in November.

Let me actually go with the clockmaker. Structure:

- Open with the strangeness: in the town of [name], no two clocks tell the same time, and this is on purpose.
- Introduce the clockmaker — let's say she's a woman, older. Or make the protagonist the outsider.
- Protagonist: someone who arrives — maybe to settle a dead parent's affairs. The parent lived there. The protagonist inherits a clock that's stopped.
- They take it to the clockmaker to be repaired. The clockmaker repairs it but won't tell them what time to set it to — that's not hers to decide.
- Protagonist learns, through observation, what the clocks mean. The baker's clock reads 4:47 — the time her husband, a fisherman, was due home and wasn't; she keeps it at the last time he was expected. Actually maybe more hopeful: the time they first met. Mix of grief and joy across the town.
- The protagonist finally realizes what moment their parent's clock was keeping — maybe there's a note, or the clockmaker remembers servicing it. The parent's clock read a specific time — say 6:12 — and the protagonist learns/knows it was the time the protagonist was born, or the time the protagonist's train left thirty years ago after a fight, the parent keeping the moment the child was still there.
- Ending: protagonist winds the clock, sets it to that time, lets it run from there. Time moves forward from the kept moment. Quiet, aching.

That's a full arc in ~1000 words. Doable if I'm economical.

Names: The town could be called something coastal or inland-generic. Let's not overload names. The clockmaker: a woman named Mrs. Halloran? Or unnamed, "the clockmaker." Protagonist: could be first-person or third. First person might be more intimate: "I came to Wellbridge to close out my mother's house." Let's do first person, unnamed protagonist.

Mother's house, mother recently died. Protagonist hasn't been back in years — a falling out, or just distance. On the mantel: a clock, stopped at 6:12. Protagonist takes it to the clockmaker because it feels wrong to sell it stopped, or because selling everything requires everything working, or simply because it was her mother's and stopping it feels like a second death.

"A clock doesn't tell you the time," she says. "It tells you time is passing. Where you start it is the only thing you get to choose."

KEPT TIME

The clock on my mother's mantel said 6:12. It had said 6:12, I would learn, for two years.

I'd come back to Fenwick to empty her house — the lawyer's phrase, as if a house were a pocket. Three weeks dead. We were not estranged, exactly. There is a distance that requires no decision, that grows the way damp rises in a wall: invisibly, until one day the paper bubbles. The calls got shorter. Then seasonal. Then a card at Christmas, signed with the kind of love that has become penmanship.

Mrs. Clee from next door came over with a lasagna and stayed to wrap plates. At some point she said, apropos of nothing I understood, "She kept her Sundays, you know. Right up to the end." I said that was nice. She looked at me a beat too long, the way you look at someone who has missed the point of a room.

"Take the clock to Vane," she added, nodding at the mantel. "She's seen to it for years. Your mother was particular about that clock."

Particular. My mother, who let the garden go and wore one coat through four winters. It was the only thing she was particular about, and I had never once noticed.

---

The clockmaker's shop smelled of oil and pine and, faintly, the sea, which is two streets from everywhere in Fenwick and interested in none of it. Inside, a hundred clocks ticked, no two agreeing. It sounded like an argument in a large family: everyone talking at once, everyone certain.

Mrs. Vane was small and square, with walnut knuckles and fingertips precise as calipers. She knew the clock before I'd set it down. "The Ashcroft mantel," she said. "She brought this in every spring. Regular as taxes. I haven't seen it since the winter before last." She said it the way you'd say someone was overdue for a haircut. Then she looked at the still pendulum a while, and said nothing about it, which I understood to be a courtesy.

"Can you fix it?"

"The movement's sound. It wants cleaning and winding." She set down her loupe. "But I can't tell you where to put the hands. That's not mine to know."

"I don't follow."

"Walk the street sometime. Aldous at the bakery keeps his at 4:47 — the hour the tide was due to give his son back. The boat was late. In that shop it is always only just late. It never gets to be gone. Garrett the barber's says 9:58, the morning, twenty years ago, he almost didn't open again. He's opened every day since. The church keeps true time — God's minutes are all equal, Father Eamons says. The rest of us rank ours."

She let me look at the arguing room.

"A clock doesn't tell you the time. Any phone can do that. A clock tells you time is passing — and the only thing you ever choose is where it starts passing from. Births, mostly. Trains. The minute before something, or the minute after. People are honest with clocks in a way they can't manage with each other."

"Then why stop one?"

She folded her caliper-fingers on the counter. "In fifty years, I've been asked to stop a clock four times. Twice for spite. Once by a man who wanted to be buried by it." She waited. "You don't know 6:12."

"Should I?"

She told it plainly, the way you tell a thing you've kept in good repair. "She came in the February before last. Cold enough to crack pipes. She asked me to clean the movement and then stop it at 6:12. I told her a stopped clock is a grief you keep in the house. She said—" the precise fingers found each other "—she said, 'It isn't stopped. It's waiting.'"

I stood there while a hundred clocks ran on from their moments. And I did know. I knew 6:12 the way you know a word you've been pretending not to hear.

I used to call on Sundays. Six-fifteen — after her program, before her tea went cold. The tea made at ten past. The chair drawn to the phone at twelve past, hands in her lap. Three minutes of a quiet house getting ready to ring. That had been the whole liturgy of us, and I had let it thin to birthdays, to a card, to penmanship — and still, every Sunday for two years, she had made the tea and drawn the chair.

She kept her Sundays. Mrs. Clee had handed me the point of the room, and I'd smiled at it over the wrapping paper.

Around me the clocks went on passing — births, departures, the minute before — passing, all of it, into the next minute. And my mother stood at 6:12 holding three of them open, like a door.

"What do I do?" I asked. It was not a question about clocks.

Mrs. Vane cleaned what wanted cleaning. Then she put the winding key in my hand. "Yours to do."

I turned the hands to 6:12 and set the pendulum swinging, and that room of arguments gained one more voice.

"It'll run on from there," she said. "It'll pass 6:15 every day, twice. And every twelve hours it comes round again to 6:12. That's the mercy of a dial, love. Nothing on it is gone. It's only round the corner."

---

The clock hangs in my kitchen now, a long way from Fenwick. It is always wrong, and I have stopped wanting it right. Twice a day it is 6:12 and someone is waiting for the phone to ring. Twice a day it is 6:15, and the call comes through.

On Sundays I make the tea at ten past and sit down at twelve past, hands in my lap, in the last quiet minute she kept for me. At 6:15 I say, "Hi, Mom. It's me," and I tell her about my week.

The clock ticks on beside me, and keeps our time.
